title: Google Review Cards For Fitness Franchises
summary: A deployment playbook for fitness franchises rolling out Google review cards across multiple clubs — covering per-club URL routing, the specific member moments that drive conversion, the peak-vs-off-peak rhythm that distorts pilot results, staff training for high-turnover reception teams, and replacement logistics for high-touch countertop prompts.
heroPoints: Fitness franchises need per-club URL routing and a sustainable reception behaviour aligned before printing at scale — neither works without the other.
Peak and off-peak club traffic change what prompt is realistic; a pilot that only covers quiet hours misleads the full rollout.
A single pilot club paired with a representative mix of high-traffic and low-traffic time windows reveals more than a broad franchise-wide launch.

sections.title: Why fitness franchises are a distinct review-programme case
sections.intro: Fitness franchises look like multi-location retail from a distance but behave very differently once the programme goes live. The member relationship is recurring, the traffic is cyclical, and reception staff rotate faster than almost any other service vertical. All three shape the card programme.
bullets: Recurring relationship: members enter the club several times a week, which creates many chances for the prompt to land — but also raises the bar for the prompt to feel natural rather than nagging.

Cyclical traffic: 6–8 am and 5–8 pm peak windows dominate; the lobby is quiet for long stretches in between. A prompt designed for the quiet hours fails in the peak; a prompt designed for the peak feels understaffed in the quiet hours.

Reception rotation: many franchise clubs rotate reception staff weekly, often between locations. Scripts and motions have to survive onboarding cycles of under two weeks, not the six-month onboarding of a hotel property.

sections.title: Per-club URL routing and the franchise admin layer
sections.intro: Franchises nearly always need a per-club review URL. Most chains converge on a self-hosted redirect layer so the URL on the card stays stable for years while individual club profiles can change.
bullets: Subdomain pattern: review.brandname.com/club-downtown, review.brandname.com/club-westside, etc. Each redirect 301s to the specific Google Business Profile review URL for that club.
Central admin: a single spreadsheet or admin panel mapping club ID to Place ID to redirect URL. Source of truth for both card printing and profile ownership audits.
New-club onboarding: create the Business Profile, wait 48 hours for indexing, capture the Place ID, add a redirect row, print the club's card batch. Written SOP prevents mistakes.
Franchisee ownership: decide at group level whether the franchisee or the franchisor owns the Google Business Profile. Ownership changes the migration path when a franchise changes hands.
Closure and migration: when a club closes or relocates, decommission the redirect (404 the short URL) so residual cards do not drive traffic to a stale profile.
Avoid brand-wide URLs: a single 'find a club' landing page on the card always underperforms per-club routing. Members are at a specific club and expect to review that specific club.

sections.title: The three member moments that drive gym reviews
sections.intro: Across the gym formats we have seen deploy review cards — boutique boxing, large-format chains, boutique pilates, 24/7 clubs — three moments generate the bulk of the conversions. Prioritise these.
bullets: Tour-conclusion moment: end of a trial tour, after the prospect has signed up or said no. The card earns a review if the tour went well; the prospect is already in an evaluation mindset.

First-visit follow-up: the second or third actual workout, once the member has formed a habit but the experience is still fresh. Staff at reception can flag new members and hand over the card at check-in.

Personal-training milestone: the tenth session, a PT block wrap-up, a weight-loss milestone. The PT is the one who hands over the card, not reception. Conversion is very high because the relationship is direct.
Lower-priority moments: renewal time (mixed reactions), cancellation (avoid), random peak check-in (prompt gets lost in the crowd).
Digital moment: a post-workout email or in-app nudge with the same review URL works as a supplement, not a replacement. The physical card still outperforms digital-only prompts by a wide margin.

sections.title: Matching card and stand format to the club layout
sections.intro: Gym reception areas vary enormously. A boutique studio has a two-metre reception counter; a big-box chain has a lobby with multiple checkpoints. Format has to match the layout, not the brand deck.
bullets: Small reception counter (boutique studios): one hand-held card kept at the desk, staff-delivered during the first-visit follow-up or tour conclusion. Premium substrate because the card is held.
Large reception lobby (big-box chains): one NFC stand at reception plus one NFC sticker at each check-in turnstile. The stand collects staff-prompted conversions; the sticker catches unprompted taps.

PT-specific card: a personalised handheld card the trainer keeps in their kit bag. Carries the PT's name and a personal message — 'review my coaching on Google if today was useful'. Much higher conversion than a generic reception card.
Tabletop at the juice bar or shake counter: optional. Members already pause there post-workout; a small card or sticker earns extra conversions without competing with the main reception prompt.
Locker-room sticker: almost never works. Members are focused on leaving, not reviewing.

Substrate choice: the reception card is handled dozens of times a day. Plain PVC wears visibly within 60–90 days; premium PVC with a soft-touch laminate lasts 6 months. Metal-look cards project brand but scratch on gym keys.

sections.title: Staff training for fast-rotating reception teams
sections.intro: A script that depends on a stable senior reception team is not a fitness-franchise script. Design for the reality that the receptionist at the desk today may not be there next month.
bullets: Script simplicity: one-sentence ask, same across every club. 'Quick Google review if today was good?' fits on a laminated desk card reception staff can glance at.
Onboarding: the prompt is part of reception training from day one, along with check-in and membership queries. New staff should deliver it by the end of week one.

Manager prompting: the club manager prompts members themselves when they pass through the lobby. Staff models the manager's behaviour; a manager who never prompts teaches the team that the programme does not matter.
PT briefing: PTs have a separate briefing focused on their personalised card. Conversion per ask is typically 3–4× higher than reception-led asks, so PT prompting earns a dedicated training track.
Weekly review: the club manager pulls Google review velocity weekly and shares it at the team stand-up. Visibility sustains the programme through staff turnover.

Franchise-wide leaderboard: a simple top-ten list across clubs converts team pride into consistent prompting behaviour. The leaderboard compares reviews per active member, not total reviews, so small clubs can compete.

sections.title: Peak, off-peak and pilot discipline
sections.intro: Fitness traffic is the most cyclical of any review-card vertical. A pilot that averages across the week can hide patterns that matter.
bullets: Peak windows: 6–8 am, 12–1 pm in city clubs, 5–8 pm. The reception team is stretched, prompts can feel rushed, and member patience is thinner.
Off-peak windows: 9 am–noon, 1–4 pm, late evening. The team has time; prompts feel natural. But volume is low, so conversion in absolute review count is smaller.
Pilot structure: four weeks at one pilot club, measured separately for peak and off-peak windows. Report conversion rate per window, not an aggregated rate.
Peak-specific design: at peak, shift toward self-serve (NFC sticker at the turnstile, stand visible at reception) rather than handoff.
Off-peak-specific design: at off-peak, lean into handoff (reception card, PT card). The quiet moments are when the relationship-based ask converts best.

Decision rule: scale only after the pilot shows a workable conversion pattern in both peak and off-peak windows. If the programme only works off-peak, the rollout plan needs peak-window adjustments before printing 5,000 cards.

sections.title: Replacement logistics and refresh rhythm
sections.intro: Gym reception is a high-touch environment. Cards and stands wear faster than in most other verticals, and a refreshed prompt converts measurably better than a worn one.
bullets: Reception card wear: visible by day 30 on plain PVC, by day 90 on soft-touch laminate, by day 120 on metal. Replacement cadence: quarterly at minimum.
Stand wear: acrylic stands yellow and crack within a year under fluorescent lighting. Plan for annual replacement.
Sticker wear: turnstile stickers lose contrast and edge adhesion within 60–90 days, especially in clubs where members swipe a keycard right next to the sticker.
Central replenishment: franchise HQ ships replacement stock quarterly. Clubs do not self-order card stock; central control keeps branding and routing consistent.
Seasonal spikes: January (new-year signup surge) requires 2–3× normal card stock. Plan the Q4 print run accordingly.
Audit rhythm: quarterly review-card health check per club. Photograph the current stand and card; if either looks worn, replace it, then retrain reception.

faq.question: Do fitness franchises need different review-card handling for peak and off-peak times?
faq.answer: Yes. Peak windows (6–8 am, 5–8 pm) are too busy for reliable staff handoffs, so the prompt has to lean toward self-serve stands and turnstile stickers. Off-peak windows support the higher-converting reception handoff and PT-prompted asks. A pilot that averages across both hides this pattern and produces a rollout plan that works in only half the day.

faq.question: What should a fitness-franchise pilot prove first?
faq.answer: Per-club URL routing, reception adoption separately in peak and off-peak windows, and the replacement cadence for high-touch countertop prompts. Pilot at one club for four weeks; measure conversion rate separately for peak and off-peak; measure card wear at week four. If any of these fails, the rollout plan needs adjustment before the chain-wide print run.

faq.question: Should each club have its own URL on the card?
faq.answer: Yes, always. A brand-wide review URL sends members through a 'pick your club' step that halves conversion and routes some reviews to the wrong profile. Per-club URL routing is not optional for franchise programmes — it is the minimum viable setup.

faq.question: What role do personal trainers play in the programme?
faq.answer: The strongest one. PT-prompted asks convert 3–4× higher than reception-led asks because the relationship is direct. Equip PTs with a personalised card carrying their name and a one-line message ('review my coaching if today was useful'). Train PTs separately; make the PT programme a visible track in the franchise leaderboard.

faq.question: How fast do reception cards wear out in a gym?
faq.answer: Plain PVC shows visible wear within 30 days of heavy reception handling. Soft-touch laminate lasts 90 days. Metal-look cards scratch on member keys within 120 days. Quarterly replacement is the default cadence; January needs an extra print run to cover the new-year signup surge.

faq.question: How should franchise HQ manage stock and refresh?
faq.answer: Central replenishment, not club-level ordering. HQ ships replacement stock quarterly based on club size and verified review velocity. Club-level ordering drifts on branding and routing consistency within months. Central control keeps the card system honest as clubs open, close and change hands.

faq.question: What is the single biggest avoidable mistake in fitness-franchise programmes?
faq.answer: Rolling out franchise-wide stock before the per-club URL routing and the peak-window prompt model are proven. Franchises that print 50,000 cards before one club has a clean four-week pilot burn the first order on rework when the URL routing or the peak prompt turns out to need fixing.
